options.explanation: TUMOR LYSIS SYNDROME (TLS): (1) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Massive, rapid lysis of neoplastic cells (classically in high-grade hematologic malignancies: Burkitt lymphoma, ALL, AML with high WBC > 100k) releases vast intracellular contents into the bloodstream: (a) HYPERKALEMIA: Intracellular K+ release causes fatal cardiac ventricular arrhythmias; (b) HYPERPHOSPHATEMIA: Nucleic acid phosphate release precipitates with calcium, causing calcium phosphate precipitation in renal tubules and severe HYPOCALCEMIA (tetany, seizures, QT prolongation); (c) HYPERURICEMIA: Purine nucleic acid catabolism into hypoxanthine and xanthine, oxidized by xanthine oxidase into URIC ACID. Uric acid has low solubility in the acidic environment of the renal distal tubules and collecting ducts, precipitating as uric acid crystals, causing intratubular obstruction and acute obstructive uropathy; (2) CAIRO-BISHOP CRITERIA: Laboratory TLS requires >= 2 metabolic abnormalities (uric acid >= 8, K >= 6, phos >= 4.5, Ca <= 7.0) within 3-7 days of chemo; Clinical TLS requires Lab TLS PLUS acute kidney injury, seizures, cardiac arrhythmia, or death; (3) THERAPEUTIC PHARMACOTHERAPY: (a) RASBURICASE (RECOMBINANT URATE OXIDASE): Recombinant enzyme that catalyzes the enzymatic breakdown of insoluble uric acid into ALLANTOIN. Allopurinol blocks NEW uric acid synthesis but DOES NOT BREAK DOWN PRE-EXISTING CIRCULATING URIC ACID. topic: Chronic Venous Insufficiency Venous Stasis Ulcer Compression Therapy
stem: A 61-year-old woman presents to the wound care clinic with a 4-month history of an aching, non-healing ulcer over her right medial lower leg. She reports that her right leg feels heavy, swollen, and tired at the end of the day, with symptoms improving after overnight elevation. She has no history of claudication or rest pain in her foot. Her medical history includes obesity (BMI 36.4 kg/m2) and a deep vein thrombosis in the right lower extremity 6 years ago following knee surgery. On physical examination, the right lower extremity demonstrates 2+ pitting edema from the mid-calf to the ankle, woody induration of the subcutaneous tissues (lipodermatosclerosis), and diffuse reddish-brown hemosiderin hyperpigmentation over the distal third of the lower leg ('gaiter distribution'). Over the right medial malleolus, there is a 3.5 x 2.5 cm shallow ulcer with irregular, sloping borders, a moist granulating base, and copious clear serous exudate. The surrounding skin is warm without erythema, fluctuance, or purulence. Bilateral dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arterial pulses are strong and easily palpable (2+). A handheld Doppler arterial evaluation demonstrates an ankle-brachial index (ABI) of 1.05 in the right lower extremity (normal reference range 0.90-1.30). Venous duplex ultrasound demonstrates severe valvular reflux (> 1,000 ms) in the right great saphenous vein and deep femoral-popliteal system, with no acute thrombus. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the definitive management of this patient's ulcer?

options.text: Perform an emergent lower extremity catheter-directed arterial revascularization
options.explanation: Arterial pulses are normal and ABI is 1.05; the ulcer is venous, not arterial; invasive arterial revascularization is completely unindicated.

options.text: Prescribe a 14-day course of oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for presumed bacterial ulcer infection
options.explanation: The ulcer has a clean granulating base without cellulitis, purulence, or systemic fever; routine antibiotics for uninfected venous ulcers do not improve healing and breed resistant bacteria.

options.text: Initiation of multi-layer graduated compression bandaging therapy (delivering 30 to 40 mm Hg at the ankle) combined with regular leg elevation and a moist wound dressing
options.explanation: CHRONIC VENOUS INSUFFICIENCY (CVI) AND VENOUS STASIS ULCERS: (1) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Incompetent venous valves (post-thrombotic syndrome or primary valvular insufficiency) and failure of the calf muscle pump cause CHRONIC VENOUS HYPERTENSION. Elevated hydrostatic pressure transmits to dermal microvascular capillary beds, causing capillary distension, endothelial gap widening, and extravasation of fluid, fibrinogen, and red blood cells. Extravasated erythrocytes degrade, releasing hemosiderin that is engulfed by dermal macrophages, producing pathognomonic REDDISH-BROWN HYPERPIGMENTATION. Chronic interstitial inflammation causes dermal and subcutaneous fibrosis (LIPODERMATOSCLEROSIS, giving the classic 'inverted champagne bottle' leg appearance). Microvascular pericapillary fibrin cuffs and leukocyte entrapment lead to local tissue hypoxia and skin ulceration; (2) CLINICAL CHARACTERISTICS OF VENOUS ULCERS: (a) Location: Classic 'GAITER AREA' (distal lower leg, especially superior to the MEDIAL MALLEOLUS); (b) Appearance: Shallow, irregular, sloping margins, beefy-red granulating base, copious exudate; (c) Symptoms: Aching pain relieved by elevation; (3) CORNERSTONE OF TREATMENT (COMPRESSION THERAPY): GRADUATED COMPRESSION THERAPY IS THE UNDISPUTED GOLD STANDARD AND FIRST-LINE THERAPY FOR VENOUS ULCERS. Randomized controlled trials demonstrate that multi-layer compression systems delivering 30 to 40 mm Hg of graduated pressure at the ankle accelerate ulcer healing rates (healing > 70-80% of ulcers within 12-24 weeks) and prevent recurrent ulceration. Mechanism: Compression reverses ambulatory venous hypertension, reduces capillary transmural pressure, clears interstitial edema, and augments calf muscle pump velocity; (4) CRITICAL PRE-REQUISITE (RULE OUT ARTERIAL DISEASE): Before applying therapeutic compression (> 30 mm Hg), ARTERIAL PERFUSION MUST BE VERIFIED WITH AN ANKLE-BRACHIAL INDEX (ABI). Compression is safe when ABI is > 0.8-0.9. If ABI is < 0.5-0.8 (mixed arterial-venous disease or severe PAD), high-pressure compression is strictly contraindicated because it causes ischemic skin necrosis and gangrene.

options.text: Strict avoidance of all compression garments due to the risk of precipitating acute deep vein thrombosis
options.explanation: Graduated compression does not cause DVT; on the contrary, compression enhances deep venous velocity, prevents venous stasis, and is the essential life-saving therapy for venous ulcer healing.

options.explanation: Dry gauze causes painful dressing adherence and desiccates granulation tissue; bed rest promotes muscle atrophy and venous stasis; active ambulation activates the calf muscle pump and accelerates healing.

stem: A 31-year-old primigravida woman at 34 weeks and 2 days gestation presents to the labor and delivery triage unit with a 6-hour history of severe, persistent throbbing frontal headache that has not responded to oral acetaminophen. She also reports blurry vision and seeing dark spots (scotoma) floating across her visual field, as well as new-onset sharp right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Her prenatal course was uncomplicated until 2 weeks ago, when her blood pressure was noted to be 134/84 mm Hg with trace proteinuria. On arrival today, she appears uncomfortable and photophobic. Vital signs: blood pressure 172/112 mm Hg (confirmed on repeat measurement 15 minutes later), heart rate 88/min, respirations 18/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination demonstrates brisk deep tendon reflexes (3+ patellar reflexes) with 2 beats of bilateral ankle clonus. Abdominal examination reveals focal tenderness to palpation over the right upper quadrant and epigastrium without peritoneal signs. Pelvic examination reveals a closed, uneffaced cervix. Fetal cardiotocography demonstrates a baseline fetal heart rate of 140/min with moderate variability, positive accelerations, and no decelerations. Laboratory evaluation reveals: platelet count 78,000/mm3 (normal 150,000-400,000), serum AST 184 U/L (normal < 35), serum ALT 192 U/L, serum total bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.3 mg/dL (baseline 0.6 mg/dL), and spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 1.2 (abnormal >= 0.3). Which of the following represents the most appropriate management plan according to American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) guidelines?

options.text: Expectant outpatient management with oral labetalol and bed rest, aiming to prolong pregnancy until 38 weeks gestation
options.explanation: Expectant management in preeclampsia with severe features beyond 34 weeks is strictly contraindicated; continuing pregnancy causes maternal intracerebral hemorrhage, hepatic rupture, placental abruption, and fetal demise.

options.text: Administration of intravenous phenytoin loading dose 15 mg/kg for seizure prophylaxis
options.explanation: Randomized controlled trials (Lucas et al., NEJM 1995) proved that magnesium sulfate is vastly superior to phenytoin and diazepam for preventing eclamptic seizures; phenytoin is ineffective and not recommended.

options.text: Emergent cesarean delivery under general anesthesia prior to administering antihypertensives or magnesium sulfate
options.explanation: Performing emergent surgery in an unstable, unmedicated patient with severe hypertension (172/112) risks catastrophic stroke and intraoperative eclamptic seizure; maternal medical stabilization must precede delivery.

options.text: Initiation of intravenous magnesium sulfate for eclampsia seizure prophylaxis, urgent intravenous antihypertensive therapy (labetalol or hydralazine) targeting blood pressure < 160/110 mm Hg, and prompt delivery following maternal stabilization
options.explanation: PREECLAMPSIA WITH SEVERE FEATURES: (1) DEFINITION AND DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA (ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222): Preeclampsia is new-onset hypertension (SBP >= 140 or DBP >= 90 mm Hg after 20 weeks gestation) with proteinuria (>= 300 mg/24hr or protein:creatinine ratio >= 0.3) OR NEW-ONSET SEVERE FEATURES IN THE ABSENCE OF PROTEINURIA: (a) Severe-range blood pressure (SBP >= 160 or DBP >= 110 mm Hg confirmed 15 min apart); (b) THROMBOCYTOPENIA (platelets < 100,000/mm3); (c) IMPAIRED LIVER FUNCTION (transaminases > 2x upper limit of normal) or severe persistent RUQ/epigastric pain; (d) RENAL INSUFFICIENCY (creatinine > 1.1 mg/dL or doubling); (e) PULMONARY EDEMA; (f) NEW-ONSET PERSISTENT HEADACHE UNRESPONSIVE TO ANALGESICS OR VISUAL DISTURBANCES (scotoma, photopsia, cortical blindness); (2) EMERGENCY PHARMACOLOGICAL STABILIZATION: (a) SEIZURE PROPHYLAXIS: INTRAVENOUS MAGNESIUM SULFATE (4 to 6 g IV loading dose over 20-30 min, followed by 1 to 2 g/hr continuous infusion). Multiple landmark randomized trials (Magpie trial) proved magnesium sulfate is the gold-standard anticonvulsant, reducing eclamptic seizures by > 50% and reducing maternal death; (b) ACUTE ANTIHYPERTENSIVE THERAPY: Mandatory within 30-60 minutes for severe-range BP (>= 160/110 mm Hg) to prevent maternal hemorrhagic stroke: IV LABETALOL, IV HYDRALAZINE, or oral immediate-release NIFEDIPINE; (3) DEFINITIVE MANAGEMENT (TIMING OF DELIVERY): (a) In preeclampsia WITHOUT severe features: Delivery at 37 weeks gestation; (b) IN PREECLAMPSIA WITH SEVERE FEATURES: DELIVERY IS INDICATED AT >= 34 WEEKS GESTATION UPON MATERNAL STABILIZATION (or at any gestational age if maternal/fetal deterioration occurs: refractory severe BP, pulmonary edema, eclampsia, placental abruption, DIC, or non-reassuring fetal status). subject: Ethics
topic: Communicable Disease Confidentiality and Partner Notification
stem: A 32-year-old married man presents to the infectious diseases clinic for follow-up of confirmatory laboratory testing. He has been married for 6 years and has two young children. Ten days ago, he underwent diagnostic testing following an episode of acute febrile illness accompanied by a transient generalized rash. Fourth-generation HIV antigen/antibody combo immunoassay and confirmatory HIV-1/HIV-2 differentiation assay are positive, and plasma HIV-1 RNA viral load is 185,000 copies/mL, establishing a new diagnosis of acute HIV infection. During post-test counseling, the physician discusses initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) immediately and emphasizes the crucial importance of notifying his wife so that she can undergo HIV testing and receive post-exposure or pre-exposure prophylaxis if appropriate. The patient becomes intensely agitated and tearful, stating: 'You cannot tell my wife. If she finds out, she will divorce me, take our children, and ruin my life. I forbid you from contacting her or revealing my diagnosis to anyone. This is between me and you, and doctor-patient confidentiality is absolute.' Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in clinical and ethical management according to American Medical Association (AMA) ethical guidelines and public health law?

options.text: Agree with the patient and maintain absolute secrecy, promising never to report the diagnosis to public health authorities or discuss it with anyone
options.explanation: Physicians are legally mandated by state statutes to report communicable diseases like HIV to public health agencies; failing to report is illegal and breaches public health safety.

options.text: Immediately telephone the patient's wife directly while the patient is still in the clinic, without informing the patient of your intention
options.explanation: Directly contacting the spouse without attempting persuasion or explaining the reporting process violates ethical protocols; the patient should be counseled, given an opportunity to disclose, and public health partner services should be engaged.

options.text: Refuse to provide antiretroviral therapy to the patient until he signs a formal written contract agreeing to tell his wife
options.explanation: Conditioning medical treatment on disclosure is unethical and coercive; the patient must receive prompt antiretroviral therapy to improve his health and lower viral load (undetectable = untransmittable), while addressing disclosure via public health channels.

options.text: Discharge the patient from the clinical practice immediately due to an irreconcilable ethical conflict of interest
options.explanation: Abandoning a newly diagnosed HIV patient is an ethical violation and harms both the patient and the community; the physician must continue care while fulfilling public health duties.

options.text: Explain to the patient that physician-patient confidentiality is not absolute when an identifiable third party is at grave risk of infectious harm, notify the state or local public health department in accordance with mandatory reporting laws, and encourage the patient to disclose or utilize health department partner notification services
options.explanation: MEDICAL ETHICS, PATIENT CONFIDENTIALITY, AND COMMUNICABLE DISEASE PARTNER NOTIFICATION: (1) PRINCIPLE OF CONFIDENTIALITY AND ITS BOUNDARIES: Doctor-patient confidentiality is a foundational cornerstone of the therapeutic relationship, fostering honest communication and trust. However, ETHICAL AND LEGAL CONSENSUS UNANIMOUSLY HOLDS THAT CONFIDENTIALITY IS NOT ABSOLUTE. Confidentiality may be breached when required by law or when an identifiable third party faces an imminent, serious, and foreseeable risk of grave bodily harm (the ethical doctrine originating in Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California); (2) AMA CODE OF MEDICAL ETHICS OPINION 3.2.1 (COMMUNICABLE DISEASE REPORTING): When a patient is diagnosed with a transmissible communicable disease (e.g., HIV, syphilis, tuberculosis), the physician has a dual duty to the patient and to public health: (a) MANDATORY REPORTING TO PUBLIC HEALTH AUTHORITIES: All states legally require healthcare providers to report new diagnoses of HIV to local or state public health departments; (b) PARTNER NOTIFICATION SERVICES: The physician must first attempt to persuade the patient to disclose their diagnosis voluntarily to at-risk sexual or needle-sharing partners. If the patient refuses, the physician must work in coordination with the public health department. In many jurisdictions, public health contact tracers utilize CONFIDENTIAL PARTNER NOTIFICATION SERVICES, contacting the spouse or partner to inform them of potential exposure and offering testing and counseling WITHOUT DISCLOSING THE IDENTITY of the infected source patient; (c) DIRECT DISCLOSURE BY PHYSICIAN: In situations where public health mechanisms are unavailable and an identifiable spouse is at immediate risk of fatal infection, physicians are legally and ethically permitted (and in some jurisdictions required) to notify the endangered third party directly, provided the patient is informed beforehand; (3) PATIENT APPLICATION: The physician must clearly explain that confidentiality cannot shield an unsuspecting spouse from fatal transmission, report the case as mandated by state public health statutes, and support the patient in disclosure or coordinate partner notification.
